findings.heading: From SAS / Basic data manipulation
findings.proposition: The translation opens the SAS row with "Veri kümesini özellikle belirtmenize gerek yoktur" (you do not need to specify the dataset), a claim the English SAS table never makes; the English row instead states that no special procedure is needed to create a variable.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader learns a false generalisation about SAS, that datasets never need naming, instead of the actual point being contrasted, which is how a new variable is created. The sentence appears to have been copied from the Stata table row (English line 182), so the reader also loses the SAS-specific contrast that motivates the R `mutate()` column beside it.

findings.heading: From SAS / Descriptive analysis
findings.proposition: The translation places "**skimr** paketinden" (from the skimr package) in front of both functions, so it states that `summary(dataset)` comes from the skimr package; the English attaches "from the **skimr** package" only to `skim(dataset)`, `summary()` being base R.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader believes `summary()` requires installing and loading skimr, and may conclude the function is unavailable without it, or fail to find `summary()` documented in the skimr reference.

findings.heading: Tidy data
findings.proposition: The English gives two examples of different pieces of information combined into one cell: multiple partner organisations in one area, AND the status "TBC" in the same cell as "Partner D". The translation keeps only the first example and drops the "TBC" / "Partner D" one.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader sees only the case of several entities crammed into one cell, and misses the second, distinct non-tidy pattern shown in the screenshot: a status value stored in the same cell as the entity it describes. That pattern is the one most likely to recur in their own spreadsheets.

findings.heading: Benefits
findings.proposition: The translation attributes the new possibilities R opens up to its varied libraries ("Birbirinden farklı kütüphaneleriyle R size yeni olasılıkların muazzam kapısını açacaktır"). The English names no cause; it simply states that an immense scope of new possibilities will open with R.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader is given a specific causal explanation, the package ecosystem, that the English chapter does not make at this point, and may expect the surrounding text to develop it.

findings.heading: Benefits
findings.proposition: The English states that the return on the time invested in the learning curve will be significant ("The dividends will be significant"). The translation omits this claim entirely.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader is told there is a learning curve costing effort, but is not told the payoff justifies that cost. The paragraph's cost-versus-benefit argument, which is the reason the section is called Benefits, loses one of its two halves.

findings.heading: From Stata / Working directory
findings.proposition: The English R column states that working directories in R can be EITHER absolute OR relative to a project root folder via the **here** package. The translation states only that they can be directed to the project root folder or other locations using the **here** package, dropping the absolute-path option.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader coming from Stata concludes that R does not support absolute paths the way Stata does, and that the **here** package is mandatory rather than one of two options.

findings.heading: From SAS / Working directory
findings.proposition: The English R column states that working directories in R can be EITHER absolute OR relative to a project root folder via the **here** package. The translation states only that they can be directed to the project root folder or other locations using the **here** package, dropping the absolute-path option.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader coming from SAS concludes that R offers no absolute-path option, and that the **here** package is required rather than one of two available choices.

findings.heading: Data interoperability
findings.proposition: The English sends the reader to the Import and export page through a working cross-reference, [Import and export](importing.qmd). The translation writes the bracketed label "[İçe ve dışa aktar]" with no link target, so the cross-reference does not exist.
findings.reader_consequence: The only substantive content of this whole section is the pointer to another page. A Turkish reader sees bare bracketed text, cannot follow it, and has no file name to search for, so the section tells them a detailed page exists but not how to reach it.

findings.heading: From SAS / General notes
findings.proposition: The translation lists three SAS comment forms, "`* METİN`; `/*` veya `/* METİN */`", presenting a bare `/*` as a comment form in its own right. The English lists exactly two: `* TEXT ;` and `/* TEXT */`.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader may take `/*` alone to be a valid SAS comment and write an unterminated block comment, which swallows the following code. The English also keeps the terminating semicolon inside the syntax; the translation moves it outside the code span, weakening the signal that `* TEXT ;` must end in a semicolon.
